title: Kaliya

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mouth full of universe, and the forgetting: Yashoda saw everything, then was given back her ordinary love. Did you simply enjoy someone familiar? Day eight hundred ninety-two.
screen: `THE MOUTH FULL OF UNIVERSE.` · `THE FORGETTING IS THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: A hot day by the Yamuna. The boy Krishna is old enough now to take the calves and cows out to graze with his friends. It's summer, and on this day Balarama isn't with them. The boys and the cattle, desperate with thirst, come down to a part of the river and drink. And they drop where they stand, cowherds and cows alike, lifeless at the water's edge. Krishna sees them. He looks at them, the text says, with a glance full of nectar, and they get up, puzzled, as if waking from sleep. Something is wrong with that water.
screen: `A HOT DAY BY THE YAMUNA.` → `THEY DRINK, AND FALL.` → `A GLANCE BRINGS THEM BACK.`

segments.voice: What's wrong with the water is Kaliya. In a deep pool of the Yamuna lives a great serpent, a naga with many hoods, and his poison has turned the pool into something boiling and deadly. The Bhagavata says birds flying over it fall out of the sky. The plants on its banks are dead. Krishna decides the river has to be made clean again. On the bank stands a tall kadamba tree. He climbs it, tightens his clothes, slaps his arms like a wrestler, and jumps, right into the poisoned pool. The water heaves. Kaliya rises, furious that someone has entered his home. He sees a small, dark, beautiful boy playing in the water, and he bites him, and wraps him in his coils. And Krishna goes still. Up in the village, the people see terrible omens, and they look for Krishna, and he isn't there. The whole village runs to the river: the women, the old men, the children, the cows. They follow his footprints to the bank and see him there, motionless, wrapped in a serpent. Yashoda wants to go into the water after him. Nanda does too. The gopis cling to her, grieving. And one person on that bank is calm. Balarama, the text says, knows his brother's power, and he holds them back, and smiles. So the chapter leaves us in a strange place. A whole village in despair on the riverbank. One brother quietly smiling. And in the water, the boy they love, perfectly still, inside the coils.
screen: `A POISONED POOL IN THE YAMUNA.` · `HE JUMPS FROM THE KADAMBA TREE.` · `THE WHOLE VILLAGE RUNS TO THE BANK.` · then, large: `BALARAMA SMILES.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your gaze drop. Bring to mind something you're watching from the bank right now: a person you love in a hard place, a situation you can't jump into and fix. Breathe with the worry for a moment, honestly. Then, without forcing it, let in a little of Balarama's calm: the possibility that more is happening in the water than you can see from here. Hold both, the worry and the calm. If you pray, you can hold that person in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Kaliya. The many-hooded serpent whose poison fills a pool of the Yamuna, and who wraps the boy Krishna in his coils.
Your line: Kaliya. Today, when you're watching something hard from the bank, take one breath of Balarama's calm before you react. Day eight hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Pilgrims in Vrindavan visit a bathing place on the Yamuna associated with Kaliya, and some festivals reenact the boy Krishna's leap into the river.

myth: Krishna falls into the pool by accident
he climbs the kadamba tree and jumps in on purpose.
the boys who drank the water are revived by Krishna's glance

the whole village stays calm on the bank
the village despairs; only Balarama is calm.

fork.setup: you're Balarama. your little brother lies motionless in the serpent's coils, and his mother wants to go into the water. what do you do?
options: hold them back, calm, knowing his power.
run for help from the next village.
fork.reveal: Balarama holds them back and smiles. he knows what his brother can do.

original.note: Sanskrit: Kaliya, the serpent of the Yamuna pool.

trapdoor: what you thought: the snake has Krishna trapped.
what it means: the village despairs, but his brother on the bank isn't worried.
what a scholar hears: the text gives the village's grief at length, and gives Balarama a single, quiet smile.
